acc-01.title: What Is Accounting?
explain: **Accounting** is the work of recording the results of economic activity as numbers, organizing them, and delivering them as **information** to the people who need it. A shopkeeper keeping a ledger and a large company issuing a report are doing the same job at different scales.

The people who use accounting information are called **information users**. Each user wants to know something different.
- Owners and managers: whether business is going well and what to change next
- Investors: whether the company is worth putting money into
- Creditors (people who lent money): whether the money they lent will be repaid on time
- Employees: whether the company is stable

The reports that gather the recorded results and present them to outsiders are called **financial statements**. The main ones are as follows.
- **Statement of financial position** (balance sheet): how much is owned and how much is owed on a particular date
- **Income statement**: how much was earned and how much was spent over a period
- **Statement of cash flows**: where cash came from and where it went over a period
- **Statement of changes in equity**: how the owner's share changed during the period

In this department we use a fictional shop, **Hanbit Bakery**, as our example. Amounts are in units of 10,000 won. This course only introduces the basic concepts of accounting; it is not a guide to tax filing, auditing, or professional exams.

acc-02.title: The Accounting Equation
explain: The skeleton of accounting is a single line: **assets = liabilities + equity**.

- **Assets**: valuable things the shop owns (cash, inventory, equipment, and so on)
- **Liabilities**: money owed to others
- **Equity**: what is left after subtracting liabilities from assets; the owner's share

The left side says what is owned; the right side says whose money was used to obtain it. The portion borrowed from others is liabilities, and the owner's portion is equity. That is why the two sides always add up to the same total.

explain: Since equity is assets minus liabilities, it can also be written **equity = assets − liabilities**. For Hanbit Bakery, 500 − 200 = 300.
The equation does not break when transactions occur. If the shop borrows 100 from a bank, cash (an asset) rises by 100 and liabilities also rise by 100, so both sides become 600 together.

acc-03.title: Recording Transactions: Debit and Credit
explain: In accounting, a **transaction** is an event that changes the amount of assets, liabilities, or equity. Each transaction is recorded in a **journal entry**. A journal entry decides which items are written on the left and which on the right. The left side is called the **debit** and the right side the **credit**. These words carry no meaning such as a bank's lending or borrowing; they are simply names for left and right.

Each type of item has a fixed side on which it increases.
- Assets, expenses: increase when written on the debit side
- Liabilities, equity, revenues: increase when written on the credit side
When they decrease, they are written on the opposite side.
Every transaction must be written so that **total debits = total credits**. This rule keeps the equation from breaking.
A table that gathers the changes for each item is a **T-account**. It is shaped like the letter T, with debits on the left and credits on the right.

explain.alt: A T-shaped table titled Cash account. On the left debit side is capital contribution 300; on the right credit side is ingredients 120; below it says remaining cash 300 − 120 = 180. On the right are two boxes. Increases when written on the debit side: assets, expenses. Increases when written on the credit side: liabilities, equity, revenues.

acc-04.title: The Income Statement
explain:
The **income statement** shows what was earned and what was spent over a period (a month, a year).
- **Revenue**: what was earned from business (sales and so on)
- **Expenses**: what was spent to earn revenue (cost of ingredients, salaries, rent, and so on)
- **Profit**: revenue minus expenses
**Profit = revenue − expenses**. If the value is negative, it is called a loss.

explain.alt: A horizontal bar picture of Hanbit Bakery's profit and loss for one month (unit: 10,000 won). Revenue, sales 800, is the longest bar, and the expenses, cost of goods sold 450, salaries 150, and rent 60, are shorter bars. Below a dotted line, a question mark is written next to the profit bar.

explain: In the figure, revenue is a single item, sales of 800, and there are three expenses: 450, 150, and 60. Adding all the expenses gives 660, and subtracting that from revenue gives the profit.

Profit increases equity. When there is profit, the owner's share, equity, grows by that amount, and when there is a loss it shrinks. This is why revenues are written on the credit side and expenses on the debit side.
One caution: profit does not necessarily mean cash increased. If goods are sold on credit, the sale is recorded, but the cash comes in later.

acc-05.title: The Statement of Financial Position
explain: The **statement of financial position** (balance sheet) shows assets, liabilities, and equity on one page as of a particular date. Assets are on the left and liabilities and equity on the right, so the totals match, just as in the accounting equation.

explain.alt: Hanbit Bakery's statement of financial position (unit: 10,000 won). The left assets column has current assets of 200 on top (cash 120, inventory 80) and non-current assets of 300 below (equipment such as ovens, 300). The right liabilities-plus-equity column has liabilities of 200 on top (money owed to others) and equity of 300 below (the owner's share). At the bottom it says total 500 = total 500.

explain:
Assets and liabilities are usually divided by how long they last.
- **Current assets**: assets that become cash or are used within one year (cash, inventory, and so on)
- **Non-current assets**: assets kept and used for a long time (equipment such as ovens, and so on)
- **Current liabilities**: liabilities that must be repaid within one year
- **Non-current liabilities**: liabilities repaid after more than one year

The profit from the previous lesson is added to equity on the statement of financial position. The difference is that the income statement shows the flow over a period, while the statement of financial position shows a picture at one point in time.
If Hanbit Bakery sells inventory of 80 for cash of 80, cash of 120 becomes 200 and inventory becomes 0. Only the composition within current assets changed, so total assets stay at 500.

acc-06.title: Reading Financial Statements
explain:
The numbers in financial statements are hard to interpret from their size alone. Dividing one number by another to make a **ratio** makes comparison easier. Two are introduced here.
- **Debt ratio** = liabilities ÷ equity × 100 (%)
- **Profit margin** = profit ÷ sales × 100 (%)
The debt ratio shows how large other people's money (liabilities) is compared with one's own share (equity). The profit margin tells how much profit there is for every 100 won of sales.

explain.alt: Bars for two shops whose assets are each 1000. Gaon Store is divided into liabilities of 600 and equity of 400; Naru Workshop is divided into liabilities of 200 and equity of 800. It says the full bar length is assets of 1000 (in 10,000 won).

explain: The two shops in the figure each have assets of 1000. Gaon Store has liabilities of 600 and equity of 400, so its debt ratio is 600 ÷ 400 × 100 = 150%. Naru Workshop has liabilities of 200 and equity of 800, so its ratio is 25%.

A high ratio cannot be called bad right away, nor can a low ratio be called good right away. The appropriate level differs by industry and period, and a business can also grow by using borrowed money. A ratio is a starting point for asking questions.
Hanbit Bakery's profit margin is 140 ÷ 800 × 100 = 17.5%, since its profit is 140 on sales of 800.

acc-07.title: The Five Steps of Revenue Recognition
explain: When should a company record sales in its books? When it receives the money? When it signs the contract? When it ships the goods? Depending on the timing, the same company's profit this year can differ greatly. If Stage 1 covered the basics of accrual accounting, this lesson covers the internationally used **five-step approach** to revenue recognition.

**(1) Identify the contract**: There must be a contract that the parties have approved, with clear rights and payment terms, and for which collecting the consideration is probable. **(2) Identify the performance obligations**: Within the contract, separate the **distinct** goods or services promised to the customer. If a mobile phone and a two-year telecom service are sold together, they are separate performance obligations.

**(3) Determine the transaction price**: This is the consideration the company expects to receive from the customer. Reflect discounts, expected returns, and variable consideration that depends on performance. **(4) Allocate the transaction price**: If there are several performance obligations, divide the transaction price in proportion to the price at which each would be sold separately (the **standalone selling price**). **(5) Recognize revenue when the performance obligation is satisfied**: Revenue is recognized when the customer gains **control** of the goods or services. Some are satisfied at **a point in time**, like delivering merchandise, and others **over time**, like a subscription service.

Why is it made so complicated? If all the payment for a bundled sale were recorded as revenue at once when the contract is signed, even the consideration for services not yet provided would enter this year's profit. The five steps prevent profit inflation by making the company recognize revenue **only to the extent it has actually transferred to the customer**. Consideration received in advance but not yet performed remains as a **contract liability** (unearned revenue).

Limitations: when a standalone selling price cannot be observed (goods sold only as a bundle), estimation is needed, and estimating variable consideration involves judgment. Where there is room for judgment, there is also room for earnings management. That is why the major judgments must be disclosed in the notes. This lesson is a conceptual introduction and is not advice on actual accounting treatment or taxes.

Step 2 (recognition): The device is recognized as 72 when delivered, and the service is recognized at 4 per month over 12 months. Right after the contract, the books show revenue of 72 and a contract liability of 48.

acc-08.title: Inventory Cost Flow: FIFO and Weighted Average
explain: The same item was bought several times at different prices. If some of it was sold, how much should the cost of what was sold (the **cost of goods sold**) be taken to be? Unless price tags are attached to the goods, there is no way to know which purchase's goods were sold. So accounting sets a **cost flow assumption**. This choice changes the cost of goods sold, profit, and the ending inventory amount.

The basic relationship is **goods available for sale = beginning inventory + purchases for the period**, and this is divided into **cost of goods sold** and **ending inventory**. How it is divided is the cost flow assumption. The **first-in, first-out method** (FIFO) assumes that what was bought first is sold first. So the ending inventory remains at the most recent purchase prices. The **weighted average method** applies the average unit cost of the goods available for sale to every unit.

Comparing the two methods in a period of **rising** prices: under FIFO, the old, cheap costs go to cost of goods sold, so cost of goods sold is low, **profit is high**, and the ending inventory is at recent, expensive prices, so the statement of financial position amount is **close to current value**. The weighted average method falls in between. In a period of falling prices it is the reverse. Under either method the total goods available for sale is the same, so the lower the cost of goods sold, the higher the ending inventory by the same amount.

Inventory is recorded at cost, but if the **net realizable value**, the selling price minus selling costs, falls below cost, an **inventory write-down** is recognized for the difference (lower of cost and net realizable value). This is because leaving inventory whose value has fallen, such as out-of-fashion clothes or food near its expiry date, at its original cost would inflate assets.

Limitations and cautions: the cost flow assumption need not match the actual flow of goods. Once a method is chosen, it must be **applied consistently** to keep comparability. Changing the method changes profit, so the change and its effect must be disclosed. Inventory amounts are directly tied to profit, which also makes it an area where accounting fraud often occurs (covered in Stage 5). This lesson is a conceptual introduction and is not advice on actual accounting or tax treatment.

acc-09.title: Property, Plant and Equipment and Depreciation
explain: If a machine to be used for 5 years is bought for 1,000 won, is that 1,000 won an expense of the year it was bought? If so, profit in the year of purchase falls sharply and profit in the other four years is inflated. The machine is used to produce revenue for five years, so it is reasonable to recognize its cost as an expense spread over the five years. This allocation process is **depreciation**.

Depreciation needs three things: the **acquisition cost** (the purchase price plus the costs of getting the asset ready for use, such as installation and transport), the **useful life** (the period it is expected to be used), and the **residual value** (the amount expected to be received on disposal at the end of the useful life). The depreciable amount is acquisition cost − residual value. The important point is that depreciation is **an allocation of cost, not a market valuation** of the asset.

explain.alt: A graph of the book value of an asset with acquisition cost of 1,000 won, residual value of 100 won, and useful life of 5 years. (1) The straight-line method falls from 1,000 by the same amount each year to 820, 640, 460, 280, and 100. (2) The declining-balance method (40%) falls from 1,000 to 600, 360, 216, and 129.6, and reaches 100 in year 5. The declining-balance method falls faster early on.

explain: The **straight-line method** depreciates the same amount each year: $(\text{취득원가} - \text{잔존가치})/\text{내용연수}$. As in figure (1), the book value falls along a straight line. The **declining-balance method** depreciates by multiplying the opening book value each year by a fixed rate. As in figure (2), more is depreciated early and less later. It suits assets that are more efficient early in use or that become obsolete quickly. There is also the **units-of-production method**, which depreciates in proportion to output.

Annual profit differs depending on the method, but the total depreciation expense over the whole useful life is the same (acquisition cost − residual value). **Depreciation is an expense with no cash outflow.** The cash already went out when the machine was bought. That is why depreciation is added back to net income in the statement of cash flows (Stage 3).

Limitations and judgment: the useful life and residual value are **estimates**. Setting a longer useful life lowers the expense each year and raises profit. When an estimate is changed, it is reflected only in later periods and its effect is disclosed. If the recoverable amount of an asset falls well below its book value, an **impairment loss** is recognized. This lesson is a conceptual introduction, and depreciation for tax purposes may differ.

acc-10.title: Financial Liabilities and the Effective Interest Method
explain: When a company issues bonds (corporate bonds), the promised interest rate (the coupon rate) can differ from the interest rate the market requires (the market rate). Then the bonds sell for less than face value (at a discount) or for more (at a premium). How does accounting spread this difference as an expense over the life of the bond? The method is the **effective interest method**. It applies to the accounting books the same principle as the bond price calculation in finance.

The issue price of a bond is the present value of the future cash flows (interest and principal) discounted at the **market interest rate at the time of issue (the effective interest rate)**. If the market rate is higher than the coupon rate, the bond is issued at a discount; if lower, at a premium. The issuing company records the amount received (the issue price) as the carrying amount of the liability.

Each period's **interest expense** is the opening carrying amount × the effective interest rate. The **cash interest** actually paid is face value × the coupon rate. In a discount issue, interest expense > cash interest, and the carrying amount rises by the difference (**amortization of the discount**). At maturity, the carrying amount reaches exactly the face value. $$\text{장부금액}_{t} = \text{장부금액}_{t-1} + (\text{이자비용} - \text{현금 이자})$$

Why is it done this way? A discount issue is in effect a contract that "pays less coupon interest but repays more at maturity than was received." That extra repayment is also part of interest, so it must be recognized as an expense over the period. The effective interest method recognizes the expense at a **constant interest rate** on the liability balance each period, so it shows the true cost of borrowing accurately.

Limitations: the effective interest rate is fixed at the time of issue, so the carrying amount does not change even if market interest rates change afterwards (amortized cost measurement). So the liability in the books can differ from its current market value. Early repayment terms or floating-rate terms make the calculation more complex. This lesson is a conceptual calculation and is not advice on actual accounting treatment.

acc-11.title: Provisions and Contingent Liabilities
explain: Companies face future expenditures whose **amount or timing is not fixed**, such as product warranty repairs, lawsuit damages, and environmental restoration. Should such an obligation be recorded as a liability in the books now? If it is reflected too late, profit and financial soundness are inflated; if it is reflected too easily, it becomes a tool for managing profit as you please ("cookie jar" reserves). Accounting has set clear criteria.

A **provision** is recognized as a liability when **all** of the following three conditions are met. (1) There is a present obligation (a legal or constructive obligation) as a result of a past event. (2) An outflow of resources to settle that obligation is **probable**. (3) The amount can be **reliably estimated**. A constructive obligation is one that is not a legal obligation, but because of the company's published policy or practice, the other party legitimately expects the company to perform it.

When the conditions are not met: if an outflow is not probable or the amount cannot be reliably estimated, it is a **contingent liability**, which is not recognized as a liability but **disclosed in the notes**. If the possibility of an outflow is remote, it is not even disclosed. Conversely, a possible gain that may be received (a **contingent asset**) is not recognized until it becomes virtually certain. This is a trace of **conservatism**: recognize losses early and gains late.

Estimating the amount: when there are many items, as with warranties, the estimate uses the **expected value** (the sum of possible outcomes × probabilities); for a single obligation such as one lawsuit, it is based on the **most likely amount**. If the expenditure is in the distant future, it is discounted to present value. The estimate is reviewed and adjusted at each closing date.

Limitations: the judgment "probable" involves subjectivity. If management rates the chance of losing an unfavorable lawsuit as low, a liability goes unrecorded. That is why auditors check the content of legal advice (Stage 5, auditing), and why investors must read the contingent liability disclosures in the notes carefully. This lesson is a conceptual introduction and is not advice on legal or accounting practice.

acc-12.title: Equity and the Statement of Cash Flows (Indirect Method)
explain: There are companies that report a profit but fail because they run short of cash. Profit and cash are different. The income statement shows profit on an accrual basis, while the **statement of cash flows** shows where actual cash came from and where it went. This lesson covers the bridge from profit to cash, the **indirect method**, and **equity**, which captures changes in the shareholders' share.

**Equity** is the shareholders' share: assets minus liabilities. Its main components are **paid-in capital** paid by shareholders (share capital and share premium), **retained earnings**, the part of profit that was not paid out as dividends and was accumulated, and other items. The change in retained earnings is $\text{기말} = \text{기초} + \text{당기순이익} - \text{배당}$. A dividend is not an expense but a **distribution** of profit, so it reduces equity, not the income statement.

The statement of cash flows divides cash flows into three activities. **Operating activities** (cash earned from the main business), **investing activities** (acquisition and disposal of equipment and securities), and **financing activities** (borrowing, repayment, share issues, dividend payments). A healthy company usually has positive operating cash flow, and uses that cash to invest or repay debt.

explain.alt: An indirect-method cash flow waterfall picture. Starting from net income of 120, it applies in turn depreciation +40, increase in accounts receivable −30, increase in inventory −20, and increase in accounts payable +10, and the last bar, cash flow from operating activities, is marked with a question mark.

explain: The **indirect method** starts from net income and adjusts it to a cash basis. (1) Non-cash expenses (depreciation) are added back. (2) If operating assets **increase, subtract** (an increase in accounts receivable means sales were made but cash was not received), and if they decrease, add. (3) If operating liabilities **increase, add** (an increase in accounts payable means an expense arose but cash has not yet been paid), and if they decrease, subtract. The figure shows this process.

A clue for analysis: if net income keeps growing but operating cash flow stays small or negative, it means receivables or inventory are piling up. It can be a warning sign that sales were recognized early or that unsold inventory is growing (earnings quality, Stage 5). Limitation: even the classification of activities in the statement of cash flows involves company choices (interest paid as operating or financing), so care is needed when comparing across companies.

acc-13.title: Cost Accounting: Job and Process Costing and Overhead Allocation
explain: A furniture factory needs to know how much it cost to make one dining table in order to set a price and know its profit. Some costs, like lumber, connect directly to a particular product, but others, like factory rent or a manager's salary, are used by several products together. **Cost accounting** is the system for assigning these costs to products.

Manufacturing costs are divided into **direct materials** (materials that can be directly traced to the product), **direct labor** (labor directly put into producing the product), and **manufacturing overhead** (costs hard to trace directly to a particular product, such as factory depreciation, electricity, and supervisors' salaries). The first two are assigned easily, but indirect costs need an **allocation base**.

**Job costing** is used for products that differ by order (custom furniture, construction projects). A cost sheet is made for each job to collect direct costs, and indirect costs are allocated using a **predetermined overhead rate**. $$\text{예정배부율} = \frac{\text{예상 제조간접원가}}{\text{예상 배부기준 총량}}$$ For example, if estimated overhead is 10 million won and estimated direct labor hours are 5,000, the rate is 2,000 won per hour. If job A used 30 hours, 60,000 won is allocated.

**Process costing** is used when the same product is produced continuously in large quantities (beverages, cement). The costs of a period are gathered and divided by the output. If there are partially completed products at period end (**work in process**), they are converted to **equivalent units** that reflect the stage of completion. 100 units that are 50% complete are treated as having used the conversion cost of 50 finished units.

Limitations: the predetermined rate is based on a forecast, so a difference from actual cost arises (an **allocation variance**), and it is adjusted at period end. A more fundamental problem is the **choice of allocation base**. If all indirect costs are allocated using direct labor hours alone, the cost of products that actually use a lot of equipment or setup work can be understated. Activity-based costing in the next lesson addresses this problem.

acc-14.title: Activity-Based Costing (ABC)
explain: A factory makes both standard products in large volumes and custom products in small volumes. Under traditional costing, the standard products showed a loss and the custom products a large profit. So the company reduced standard products and increased custom products, yet total company profit actually fell. What went wrong? Indirect costs were **allocated wrongly**. **Activity-based costing** (ABC) fixes this problem.

The traditional method allocates all indirect costs using **a single base proportional to volume**, such as direct labor hours. But a considerable portion of indirect costs arises not from volume but from the **number of activities**. Machine setup costs money each time a changeover occurs, however many units are made; quality inspection is needed for each lot, and design changes for each kind of product. Low-volume, many-variety products have small volume but use many of these activities.

The ABC procedure: (1) Identify the **activities** that generate indirect costs (setup, inspection, purchase orders, design). (2) Collect the cost of each activity (**activity cost pool**). (3) Determine the **cost driver** that measures the quantity of the activity (number of setups, number of inspections). (4) Activity rate = activity cost ÷ total quantity of the cost driver. (5) Allocate according to the quantity of the cost driver the product used.

As a result, ABC usually **lowers** the cost of high-volume products and **raises** the cost of low-volume, complex products. This is because under the traditional method high-volume products end up bearing part of the indirect costs of low-volume products, a **cross-subsidy**. Accurate cost is the basis for pricing, product mix, and process improvement (reducing costly activities).

Limitations: ABC costs a lot of money and time to identify activities and measure drivers. If activities are divided too finely, the management burden exceeds the benefit. Also, not every indirect cost is clearly linked to an activity (such as head office administration costs), so some arbitrary allocation remains. It is most effective in companies with a large share of indirect costs and a wide variety of products.

Step 2 (ABC): 30,000 won per setup, 10,000 won per inspection. Standard product $5 \times 3 + 10 \times 1 = 25$, custom product $15 \times 3 + 30 \times 1 = 75$ (in units of 10,000 won). The custom product's actual indirect cost was 7.5 times as much.

acc-15.title: CVP Analysis and Relevant-Cost Decisions
explain: How many must be sold to avoid a loss? What happens to profit if the price is lowered? Should a special order be accepted? The core tools of management accounting, **cost-volume-profit (CVP) analysis** and the concept of **relevant cost**, answer these questions.

Costs are divided into **variable costs** (such as materials), which change with sales volume, and **fixed costs** (such as rent), which do not depend on sales volume. The selling price minus the unit variable cost is the **unit contribution margin**, the amount each unit sold contributes toward covering fixed costs and then profit. Profit $= (\text{가격} - \text{단위 변동비}) \times \text{판매량} - \text{고정비}$. The sales volume at which profit is zero is the **break-even point**. $$Q_{BEP} = \frac{\text{고정비}}{\text{단위 공헌이익}}$$

explain.alt: Horizontal axis is sales volume (units, 0 to 400) and vertical axis is amount (won, 0 to 20,000). The total revenue line (50 won per unit) starts at the origin and reaches 20,000 won at 400 units. The total cost dotted line starts at fixed costs of 4,000 won and reaches 16,000 won at 400 units. The two lines meet at point P, at sales volume 200 units and amount 10,000 won. There is also a horizontal dotted line for fixed costs of 4,000 won.

explain: To earn a target profit, you must sell $Q = \frac{\text{고정비} + \text{목표 이익}}{\text{단위 공헌이익}}$ units. Using the **contribution margin ratio** (unit contribution margin ÷ price), the break-even point in sales amount = fixed costs ÷ contribution margin ratio. How far actual sales volume exceeds the break-even point is called the **margin of safety**. A company with a large share of fixed costs sees its profit swing sharply with changes in sales volume (**operating leverage**).

**Relevant cost**: in a decision, only **future costs and revenues that differ between alternatives** should be considered. **Sunk costs** already spent and costs that are the same under every alternative are irrelevant. For example, when a factory with spare capacity decides whether to accept a **special order** priced below the normal price, fixed costs are the same whether or not the order is accepted, so they are irrelevant. If the order price is higher than the **unit variable cost**, profit increases.

Limitations: CVP assumes that the price and unit variable cost are constant, that costs divide cleanly into variable and fixed, and that production equals sales. When sales volume changes greatly, non-linear effects such as volume discounts and additional equipment arise. In a special order decision too, if capacity is full, the **opportunity cost** of giving up existing orders must be included, and long-term effects, such as existing customers demanding price cuts, must also be considered.

examples.title: The Break-Even Point in the Figure
body: Conditions: the figure. Price 50 won, fixed costs 4,000 won. The total cost line is 16,000 won at 400 units, so the unit variable cost $= (16000 - 4000)/400 = 30$ won.
Step 1: Unit contribution margin $50 - 30 = 20$ won, break-even point $4000/20 = 200$ units (sales of 10,000 won). This is point P in the figure.
Step 2: For a target profit of 2,000 won, $(4000 + 2000)/20 = 300$ units must be sold.

examples.title: Judging a Special Order
body: Conditions (fictional): Normal price 50 won, unit variable cost 30 won, fixed cost allocated per unit 15 won. There is spare capacity. A customer orders 500 units at 38 won each.
Step 1: The only relevant cost is the variable cost of 30 won. Profit rises by 8 won per unit, 4,000 won in total.

Step 2: The judgment "38 won < 45 won (variable cost plus fixed cost allocation), so it is a loss" wrongly includes fixed costs. However, the risk that existing customers demand the same discount must be weighed separately.

checks.hint: Which cost does not differ between the alternatives?

Additional packaging and shipping costs

checks.prompt: In two or three sentences, explain what changes in judging a special order when production capacity is already full, compared with when there is spare capacity.
checks.hint: What must be given up to accept a new order in a full factory?
checks.explanation: Relevant cost includes not only expenditures but also the profit given up.
checks.model: When there is spare capacity, a special order raises profit as long as its price is higher than the unit variable cost. But when capacity is full, accepting the special order means giving up an existing regular order, so the contribution margin of the regular order given up is added as an opportunity cost. The special order should therefore be accepted only if its price is higher than the variable cost plus the contribution margin forgone.

acc-16.title: Ratio Analysis and DuPont Decomposition
explain: Financial statements are a sea of numbers. Two companies with sales of 100 billion won and 10 billion won cannot be compared in raw numbers. **Financial ratios** divide numbers by one another to cancel out size, making it possible to compare profitability, efficiency, and stability. If Stage 1 began reading financial statements, this lesson covers **DuPont decomposition**, which links the ratios systematically.

The main groups of ratios: **Profitability**: net profit margin (net income/sales), return on assets ROA (net income/total assets), return on equity ROE (net income/equity). **Efficiency**: total asset turnover (sales/total assets), inventory turnover (cost of goods sold/average inventory), accounts receivable turnover. **Stability**: debt ratio (liabilities/equity), current ratio (current assets/current liabilities), interest coverage ratio (operating income/interest expense).

From a shareholder's point of view, the most important indicator is **ROE**. DuPont decomposition splits ROE into the product of three factors. $$ROE = \frac{\text{순이익}}{\text{매출}} \times \frac{\text{매출}}{\text{총자산}} \times \frac{\text{총자산}}{\text{자기자본}}$$ That is, **profitability** (net profit margin) × **efficiency** (total asset turnover) × **leverage** (financial leverage). The numerators and denominators cancel in turn, leaving net income/equity.

explain.alt: A DuPont decomposition picture. The top box "Return on equity ROE = ?" is connected to three boxes below: net profit margin (net income/sales = 5%) × total asset turnover (sales/total assets = 1.2 times) × financial leverage (total assets/equity = 2.5 times).

explain: The value of the decomposition lies in showing that **the same ROE can have different sources**. Whether an ROE of 15% came from a high margin (a premium brand), from fast turnover (a discount store), or from high debt gives it entirely different meaning and risk. An ROE pushed up by debt drops sharply when business worsens, and the risk of bankruptcy is also large.

Limitations: ratios are meaningful only when there is something to **compare with** (the same company's past, competitors in the same industry). The normal level differs greatly by industry (a bank's leverage versus a manufacturer's leverage). Ratios come from accounting numbers, so differences in accounting policy or distortions pass straight through. Using the statement of financial position at a single point, year-end, can be distorted by seasonality, so averages are sometimes used. This lesson is a conceptual introduction and is not investment advice.

examples.title: The DuPont Decomposition in the Figure
body: Conditions: the figure. Net profit margin 5%, total asset turnover 1.2 times, financial leverage 2.5 times.
Step 1: $ROE = 0.05 \times 1.2 \times 2.5 = 0.15$, that is, 15%.
Step 2: ROA is the product of the first two factors, $0.05 \times 1.2 = 6\%$. Leverage of 2.5 times raised an ROA of 6% to an ROE of 15%.

examples.title: The Same ROE, Different Sources
body: Conditions (fictional): Company X: net profit margin 15%, turnover 0.5, leverage 2 → ROE 15%. Company Y: net profit margin 2%, turnover 2.5, leverage 3 → ROE 15%.

Interpretation: X is high-margin, low-turnover (luxury-goods type); Y is low-margin, high-turnover, high-leverage (retail type). If Y's sales fall a little or interest rates rise, its ROE can swing widely.

acc-17.title: Earnings Quality and Accruals: Reading Warning Signs of Distortion
explain: Two companies reported exactly the same net income of 10 billion won. For one company, nearly all of that profit came in as cash; for the other, almost no cash came in. Which profit is more trustworthy? **Earnings quality** refers to how faithfully and how sustainably reported earnings reflect actual economic performance.

Accrual-basis profit is cash flow plus **accruals**. $$\text{발생액} = \text{당기순이익} - \text{영업활동 현금흐름}$$ Accruals reflect timing differences between cash and profit, such as an increase in accounts receivable, an increase in inventory, and changes in accrued expenses. Accruals themselves are normal, but when **accruals are large and keep growing**, there is a greater risk that the profit will not be realized as cash in the future. Studies have reported a tendency for the profits of firms with a large share of accruals to be less persistent.

**Warning signs**: (1) Net income grows but operating cash flow stagnates or declines. (2) Accounts receivable grow much faster than sales (sales recognized early, uncollectible sales). (3) Inventory grows faster than sales (unsold inventory, understated costs). (4) Frequent changes in accounting estimates, such as extending useful lives. (5) Repeated one-time gains. (6) Sales concentrated at quarter end. These signs are not **evidence** of fraud; they are **reasons to investigate further**.

Examples of analysis tools: **Days sales outstanding** $= \frac{\text{매출채권}}{\text{매출}} \times 365$ days. If the collection period suddenly lengthens, suspect looser sales terms or fictitious sales. **Days inventory held** $= \frac{\text{재고}}{\text{매출원가}} \times 365$ days. Compare with the industry average or past trend to find outliers.

Limitations and balance: a growing company may normally see receivables and inventory rise and have large accruals. Do not conclude from a single sign; look at several signs together and check whether they fit the business description (a large new customer, seasonality). This lesson is a conceptual analysis and is not a judgment on whether a particular company committed fraud, nor investment advice.

examples.title: Comparing Accruals
body: Conditions (fictional): Company A net income 100, operating cash flow 95. Company B net income 100, operating cash flow 10.
Step 1: Accruals are 5 for A and 90 for B.
Step 2: Most of B's profit has not yet become cash. B's changes in accounts receivable and inventory, and its accounting policies, need further investigation.

examples.title: Trend in the Collection Period
body: Conditions (fictional): Sales are the same at 36.5 billion won, but accounts receivable were 3 billion won last year and 6 billion won this year.
Step 1: The collection period was 30 days last year and 60 days this year.

Step 2: With the same sales, collection has become twice as slow. Check the possibility that sales were made to customers from whom payment is hard to collect, or that sales not actually delivered were pulled forward.

checks.prompt: With net income of 250 and operating cash flow of 80, what are the accruals?
checks.hint: Net income − operating cash flow.

checks.prompt: With annual sales of 73 billion won and accounts receivable of 10 billion won, what is the days sales outstanding? (days)
checks.hint: (accounts receivable/sales) × 365

checks.prompt: Which of the following is the hardest to regard as a warning sign about earnings quality?
checks.hint: Look for the case in which things move in balance with each other.
checks.explanation: Balanced growth can be seen as a normal increase in accruals.
options: Sales grew 5% but accounts receivable grew 60%
Net income grew for three years in a row while operating cash flow kept falling
Sales, accounts receivable, and inventory all grew at similar rates, and operating cash flow also grew
The useful life of property, plant and equipment was suddenly extended by a large amount

checks.prompt: What is the most appropriate analytical attitude toward a company with large accruals?
checks.hint: Distinguish signs from evidence.
checks.explanation: A sign is a starting point for investigation, not a conclusion.
options: Conclude that fraud is certain
Treat it as a warning sign and investigate further whether accounts receivable, inventory, changes in accounting estimates, and the business description fit together
Ignore accruals because they are meaningless
There is no need to look at the statement of cash flows

checks.prompt: In two or three sentences, explain why "net income rose but operating cash flow fell" is a warning sign about earnings quality.
checks.hint: Think about where the gap between profit and cash is "tied up."
checks.explanation: Profit not backed by cash may be less reliable.
checks.model: The gap between net income and operating cash flow is accruals, so cash flow falling while profit rises means that accruals have grown. This means that working capital that has not yet been realized as cash, such as accounts receivable or inventory, is piling up. Such profit may later go uncollected or lead to inventory losses, so its persistence and reliability may be low.

acc-18.title: Auditing Basics: The Audit Risk Model
explain: Can financial statements prepared by a company be used on the company's word alone? Management has an incentive to show good results. So an independent outside professional reviews whether the financial statements are **free of material misstatement** under the accounting standards, and gives an opinion. This is an **audit**. This lesson covers the basic logic of auditing at a conceptual level. It has nothing to do with audit practice or professional qualifications.

An audit does not guarantee that financial statements are "perfect." Not every transaction can be examined, so the aim is **reasonable assurance**. The standard is **materiality**. Only misstatements large enough to change the judgment of information users are at issue. For example, there is a practice of setting materiality at about 5% of pre-tax profit. Audit opinions are generally divided into unqualified (no problems), qualified (problems in part), adverse (pervasive misstatement), and disclaimer (insufficient basis to form a judgment).

An auditor must decide where to look, and how deeply, in limited time. The framework for that is the **audit risk model**. $$AR = IR \times CR \times DR$$ **Audit risk** (AR) is the risk of giving an unqualified opinion when there is a material misstatement. **Inherent risk** (IR) is the risk that a misstatement arises assuming no controls (complex estimates, easily stolen assets such as cash); **control risk** (CR) is the risk that the company's internal controls fail to prevent or catch a misstatement; **detection risk** (DR) is the risk that the audit procedures fail to catch a misstatement.

The first two risks (IR, CR) cannot be changed by the auditor, who can only **assess** them. What the auditor can adjust is detection risk. To keep the target audit risk low (for example 5%), the higher the inherent and control risk in an area, the **lower** the detection risk must be set. That means enlarging samples, collecting stronger evidence (external confirmations, physical inspection), and performing procedures closer to the closing date. The warning signs from the previous lesson are factors that raise inherent risk.

Limitations: an audit relies on samples and judgment, so it cannot find all fraud. Fraud that management colludes in and conceals elaborately is especially hard to find. Also, the structure in which the auditor is paid by the company can raise independence issues, so there are systems such as rules on rotating auditors and restrictions on non-audit services.

examples.title: Setting Detection Risk With the Audit Risk Model
body: Conditions (fictional): Target audit risk 5%. Inherent risk in the sales area 80%, control risk 50%.

Step 2: If controls are weaker and control risk is 100%, $DR = 0.05/0.8 = 6.25\%$. Detection risk must be cut in half, so stronger procedures such as larger samples and external confirmations are needed.

examples.title: The Materiality Threshold
body: Conditions (fictional): Pre-tax profit 4 billion won, materiality threshold 5%.

Interpretation: Materiality is about 200 million won. A misstatement larger than 200 million won (or the sum of smaller misstatements) is judged able to change users' judgment and is examined intensively. However, matters that are material by nature, such as fraud by management, are handled separately even when the amount is small.

checks.prompt: With a target audit risk of 4%, inherent risk of 50%, and control risk of 40%, what detection risk is acceptable? (%)
checks.hint: DR = AR/(IR × CR)

checks.prompt: Match each component of audit risk with its description.
checks.hint: Only one of them can be adjusted by the auditor.
checks.explanation: The auditor assesses IR and CR and adjusts DR through procedures.
pairs: The risk that a misstatement arises because of the nature of the account itself, assuming no controls
The risk that the company's internal controls fail to prevent or catch a misstatement
The risk that audit procedures fail to catch a misstatement that remains

checks.prompt: Both the inherent risk and the control risk of an area have been assessed as high. What is the correct response by the auditor?
checks.hint: To keep AR constant, what must DR be when IR × CR is large?
checks.explanation: The higher the risk in an area, the more the substantive procedures are strengthened.
options: Set detection risk high and reduce procedures
Set detection risk low, enlarge samples, and collect stronger evidence
Do not audit that area
Raise the audit risk target

checks.prompt: What is the problem with the understanding that "audited financial statements have no errors at all"?
checks.hint: Recall the concepts of reasonable assurance and materiality.
checks.explanation: It is important to understand accurately what level of assurance an audit provides.
options: There is no problem
An audit is reasonable assurance based on samples and judgment; it is an opinion that there is no material misstatement, not a guarantee that there are no errors at all
An audit deliberately leaves errors in place
An audit is the same as a tax investigation

acc-19.title: Integrated Problem Solving: Diagnosing a Fictional Company's Financial Statements
explain: The first lesson of the capstone uses the tools from Stages 2 to 5 together on two years of summary financial data for a fictional company, "Saebyeok Foods." The goals are (1) checking earnings quality, (2) DuPont analysis, and (3) supporting a management decision (a special order). All figures are fictional.

**Data**: Sales rose from 1,000 last year to 1,100 this year (a 10% increase). Net income went from 50 to 77. Operating cash flow went from 60 to 20. Accounts receivable went from 100 to 220. Inventory went from 80 to 140. Total assets went from 800 to 1,000, and equity stayed at 400 in both years. The useful life of property, plant and equipment was extended this year from 8 years to 12 years (an effect of reducing depreciation by 15).

**Step 1 (earnings quality)**: Accruals were $-10$ last year and jumped to $77 - 20 = 57$ this year. Sales rose 10%, while accounts receivable rose 120% and inventory rose 75%. The collection period doubled from $100/1000 \times 365 = 36.5$ days to $220/1100 \times 365 = 73$ days. The useful-life extension explains 15 of the 27 increase in net income. Several warning signs overlap.

**Step 2 (DuPont)**: Last year's ROE $= 50/400 = 12.5\%$ (net profit margin 5% × turnover 1.25 × leverage 2.0). This year's ROE $= 77/400 = 19.25\%$ (net profit margin 7% × turnover 1.1 × leverage 2.5). The rise in ROE came from an improved net profit margin (a large part of which is the effect of the change in estimate) and increased leverage, while asset efficiency (turnover) actually got worse.

**Step 3 (decision)**: Saebyeok Foods' flagship product has a price of 2,000 won, a unit variable cost of 1,200 won, and annual fixed costs of 400 million won. The break-even sales volume is $4\text{억}/800 = 50$ ten-thousand units (500,000 units). With spare capacity, a large customer has requested 100,000 units at 1,400 won each. On a relevant-cost basis, that is 200 won per unit, a total profit increase of 20 million won. However, given the sharp rise in accounts receivable seen in Step 1, this customer's **collection risk** and payment terms must be weighed as well.

**Synthesis**: The first step is to check whether an "improvement" seen in the numbers is a real improvement. Earnings quality signs → identify the sources through DuPont decomposition → consider cash collection in the decision. **Critique**: A sign is not a conclusion. The rise in receivables could be due to the normal payment terms of a large new customer, so the breakdown by customer and the subsequent collection record should be checked.

examples.title: Removing the Effect of the Change in Estimate
body: Conditions: Of this year's net income of 77, the effect of the useful-life extension is 15.
Step 1: Net income on the pre-change basis $= 77 - 15 = 62$, a net profit margin of about 5.6%.
Step 2: On a comparable basis, $= 62/400 = 15.5\%$. A large part of the reported 19.25% came from the change in accounting estimate.

examples.title: The Special Order From a Cash Perspective

Interpretation: Accounting profit is recognized at the time of sale, but the cash comes in half a year later. With receivables already surging, the working capital burden and the collection risk grow. This gives grounds to negotiate terms such as an advance payment or credit insurance.

checks.hint: Fixed costs / unit contribution margin
checks.explanation: 400 million / 800 won = 500,000 units.

checks.hint: Recall the metric used for each finding.
checks.explanation: Several tools build one consistent story.

Judging whether the special order increases profit

checks.hint: Distinguish signs from conclusions.
checks.explanation: An analysis should be reported in wording that matches the level of the evidence.

acc-20.title: Bachelor's Capstone: Financial Statement Diagnosis Report
explain: The final task is to **set up two years of summary financial data for a fictional company yourself, diagnose it with the tools from Stages 2 to 5, and write a report**. It is not a task of evaluating a real company, and it is not advice for investment, tax, or audit judgments.

Report framework: (1) **Company and data setup**: industry, two years of sales, net income, operating cash flow, major assets, and equity (fictional). (2) **Accounting policy check**: timing of revenue recognition, inventory cost flow, depreciation method and changes in estimates. (3) **Earnings quality**: accruals, receivable and inventory turnover, warning signs. (4) **DuPont analysis**: the sources and changes of ROE. (5) **Decision support**: one CVP or relevant-cost analysis. (6) **The auditor's view**: high-risk accounts and the additional checks needed. (7) **Conclusion and limitations**: wording that matches the level of evidence.

Features of a good report: it starts from the numbers and moves to interpretation. It separates signs from conclusions. It cross-checks whether several indicators point in the same direction. It separates out changes in accounting policy and estimates to create "comparable" numbers. The conclusion states the remaining uncertainty and the additional data to be checked.
This task is not graded. What you submit is saved only on this device and can be viewed again under "Writings I left" in "My Progress."

examples.title: Model Outline Summary: A Fictional Online Education Company
body: Policy: One-year subscription fees are received in advance and revenue is recognized over the period. Contract liabilities are 40% of sales.

Earnings quality: Operating cash flow > net income (the effect of advance receipts). Accruals are negative, so earnings quality looks good. However, if new sign-ups decline, there is a risk that future cash will drop sharply.
DuPont: net profit margin 12%, turnover 0.8, leverage 1.5 → ROE 14.4%.
Decision: developing a new course (fixed costs 100 million won), contribution margin of 20,000 won per course enrollment → break-even of 5,000 students.
Audit view: allocation of revenue recognition over the period and the refund provision are high-risk areas.

examples.title: Example Conclusion Sentences
body: A weak conclusion: "This company is good/bad."

A good conclusion: "ROE is stable at 14%, but the decline in new subscribers has continued for two quarters, so a decrease in contract liabilities may reduce operating cash flow next year. Further checks with monthly sign-up and cancellation data are needed."

checks.explanation: It is 14.4%.

We need to check whether this is stock secured in advance of a new product launch or an accumulation of unsold old models.
